key_terms.meaning: not more than 10⁻⁹ per flight hour (hazardous 10⁻⁷, major 10⁻⁵)
independent channels: P(all lost) = P₁ⁿ, e.g. (2 × 10⁻⁴)³ = 8 × 10⁻¹²
a box swapped on the flight line with hand tools and a short test
shared cabinets of modules host many functions as partitions
fixed time window and protected memory; U = Σtᵢ ÷ T<sub>MF</sub>
screens drawn by display computers replace single-function dials
attitude, speed, altitude, vertical speed, heading, FMA; trend arrow = speed in 10 s
first electronic attitude and situation displays; now the PFD attitude area and the navigation display
Boeing and Airbus engine and crew-alerting screens
symbols focused at infinity; IFOV = 2 arctan(D ÷ 2L)
γ = arctan(V<sub>v</sub> ÷ V<sub>g</sub>), 1 kt = 101.27 ft/min
worst case = scan time − one dwell
32-bit words, 100 or 12.5 kbit/s, one transmitter to 20 receivers; T<sub>w</sub> = 36 ÷ R
1 Mbit/s, 20 µs words, one BC and up to 31 RTs, response 4 to 12 µs
B = 8 × Lmax ÷ BAG; BAG 1 to 128 ms, Lmax 64 to 1518 bytes
NA = √(n₁² − n₂²); sin θc = n₂ ÷ n₁
A catastrophic (MC/DC) to E no effect; MC/DC needs at least n + 1 tests
GF = (ΔR ÷ R) ÷ ε; full bridge output = V<sub>ex</sub> × ΔR ÷ R
emf depends on hot minus cold junction temperature; needs cold-junction compensation
G = 1 + 2R ÷ R<sub>G</sub>; rejects common-mode voltage
Q = V<sub>ref</sub> ÷ 2<sup>N</sup>; code = floor(V<sub>in</sub> ÷ Q)
across an inductive coil, cathode to +supply; clamps the L di/dt spike

takeaways: The platform sets the priorities: airliners buy safety and regularity, fighters mission and survivability, spacecraft autonomy, UAVs low size, weight and power.
Independent channels multiply reliability (2 × 10⁻⁴ becomes 8 × 10⁻¹² for three), but only if common causes are designed out.
IMA saves mass, power and wiring by sharing modules, and keeps functions apart with time and memory partitions that must fit inside the major frame.
Glass cockpits regroup the basic six onto the PFD and add maps and alerts, at the price of dependence on power, computers and software, so reversion, standby instruments and load shedding matter.
HUD symbols are collimated to infinity and conformal symbols must be boresighted; HMDs need fast head trackers.
ARINC 429 is one-way and labelled (36 bit times per word with the gap); 1553B is command/response at 20 µs per word; AFDX reserves 8 × Lmax ÷ BAG per virtual link on two parallel networks.
DO-178B sets the effort by the failure condition, and the V-model traces every requirement to code and tests both ways.
Accuracy is set at the transducer and the conditioning chain: bridge, instrumentation amplifier, anti-alias filter and ADC resolution must be designed together.
bank_note: The exam course for this unit stresses the electronics and sensing chapters (diodes, transistors, op-amps, ADCs and DACs, microcontrollers and transducers) and the evolution of civil and military aircraft electronics; most syllabi also ask for a data-bus comparison and the display formats. Every long answer below works its numbers in full and ends with a check.

bank.q: Trace the evolution of aircraft electronic systems from the valve era to integrated modular avionics, and compare the design drivers of civil and military avionics. A flight-control channel has a failure rate of 1 × 10⁻⁴ per flight hour; show how many independent channels meet a 10⁻⁹ per flight hour target.
outline: Four eras: valves, transistors, digital buses and screens, integration
Organisation framework by function
Civil drivers: safety targets, regularity, cost
Military drivers: mission, survivability, environment, EW
Redundancy calculation against 10⁻⁹ with the independence caveat
answer: Valve era (1920s to 1950s). Radios used vacuum tubes; instruments were mechanical or pneumatic and stood alone. Each function had its own box and its own wires.

Transistor era (1950s and 1960s). Transistors made radios, autopilots and fire-control computers smaller, cooler and more reliable. Analog computers ran control loops and inertial navigation reached long-range aircraft.

Digital era (1970s and 1980s). Microprocessors put functions into software. Digital buses replaced wire bundles: MIL-STD-1553 (first issued 1973) on military aircraft and ARINC 429 on airliners. Screens began replacing dials in the early 1980s, engine and alerting screens let two pilots do a flight engineer's job, and the A320 (1988) brought digital fly-by-wire to airliners.

Integrated era (1990s onward). Functions share computers: a shared cabinet on the Boeing 777 (1995) and integrated modular avionics on switched Ethernet on the A380 (2007) and 787 (2011). Military aircraft moved to integrated systems that fuse radar, infrared and radio data into one picture.

Organisation framework. Avionics is grouped by function: communication, navigation and surveillance; flight control and flight management; displays and crew interface; aircraft systems management; and, on military aircraft, mission systems (radar, EO/IR, electronic warfare, stores management).

head: Driver
Civil
Military
rows: safety, regularity, low cost of ownership
failure probability by severity: catastrophic ≤ 10⁻⁹, hazardous ≤ 10⁻⁷, major ≤ 10⁻⁵ per flight hour
high g, vibration, heat, jamming (MIL-STD-810, MIL-STD-461)
identical or dissimilar duplex and triplex channels

answer: Redundancy calculation. With λ = 1 × 10⁻⁴ per flight hour and t = 1 h, one channel fails with P₁ ≈ λt = 1 × 10⁻⁴.

answer.text: Independent channels are all lost with probability P₁ⁿ:
answer.pre:
simplex  P = 1 × 10⁻⁴      fails 10⁻⁹
duplex   P = (10⁻⁴)² = 1 × 10⁻⁸   fails 10⁻⁹ (10 times too high)
triplex  P = (10⁻⁴)³ = 1 × 10⁻¹²  meets 10⁻⁹ with a factor of 1000 spare

answer: Caveat. Squaring and cubing hold only for independent failures. A shared power supply or the same software fault in all channels is a common cause, so designers separate power, wiring routes and sometimes use dissimilar hardware or software.

Spacecraft and UAV contrast. Spacecraft avionics adds radiation tolerance and fault detection, isolation and recovery because no repair is possible; UAV avionics trades redundancy against size, weight and power and needs lost-link behaviour, so the same redundancy calculation gives a different answer once endurance is counted.
Closing check. 10⁻¹² ÷ 10⁻⁹ = 10⁻³, so the triplex system is a thousand times better than required; the duplex system at 10⁻⁸ is ten times worse. Three channels is the minimum.

bank.q: Compare federated and integrated modular avionics under mass, power, wiring, fault containment and certification. Ten federated LRUs of 2.5 kg and 35 W each are replaced by a 7 kg, 110 W cabinet. One core module runs ARINC 653 partitions of 12, 10, 6 and 4 ms in a 40 ms major frame. Find the savings, the utilisation, the partition rate, and whether a new 6 ms partition fits.
outline: Definitions: LRU, federated, IMA, partition, backplane
Comparison table
Mass and power savings with percentages
Major-frame utilisation, rate and fit test
Redundancy and common-mode faults in IMA
answer: Federated. Each function has its own LRU with its own power supply, case, cooling and point-to-point wiring. A fault stays inside one box, so it is easy to isolate and each box is certified alone.

IMA. A few cabinets hold core processing, input/output and power supply modules on a backplane. Each function runs in an ARINC 653 partition with a fixed time window in a repeating major frame and its own protected memory, so a faulty function cannot steal time or overwrite data (robust partitioning).

head: Criterion
Federated
IMA
rows: platform once, then each hosted function and the integration
higher: one module carries several functions

answer.pre:
federated mass  = 10 × 2.5 kg = 25 kg      saved 25 − 7 = 18 kg  (18 ÷ 25 = 72 %)
federated power = 10 × 35 W = 350 W       saved 350 − 110 = 240 W (240 ÷ 350 = 68.6 %)

used        = 12 + 10 + 6 + 4 = 32 ms
utilisation = 32 ÷ 40 × 100 = 80 %   spare 8 ms
rate        = 1 ÷ 0.040 s = 25 Hz for every partition

answer: New 6 ms partition. 32 + 6 = 38 ms ≤ 40 ms, so it fits, raising utilisation to 38 ÷ 40 = 95 % and leaving 2 ms. Whether that is acceptable depends on the margin policy of the platform; many designers keep spare time for growth, so the answer should state the 2 ms left.

Redundancy in IMA. Because one module now hosts several functions, a module or cabinet fault is common-mode. The two copies of a critical function go to modules in different cabinets with separate power, and standby modules are kept. IMA saves boxes, not redundancy.
Maintenance. Both rely on BITE: power-up, continuous and initiated tests store fault codes that a central maintenance computer reports, so the right LRU or module is replaced on the apron.

Spares and dispatch. Federated aircraft stock many different part numbers; IMA stocks a few module types, any of which can be loaded with the right software, which simplifies the spares pool at every station.
Closing check. 7 kg + 18 kg = 25 kg and 110 W + 240 W = 350 W; 12 + 10 + 6 + 4 + 6 + 2 = 40 ms.

bank.q: Describe the layout and content of the primary flight display, the navigation display and the EICAS or ECAM screens of a glass cockpit, and say which jobs the older EADI and EHSI did. An aircraft at 160 kt accelerates at 0.9 kt/s; an EHSI in VOR mode shows the CDI 2 dots right at 5° per dot, 30 NM from the station. Find where the speed trend arrow points and the distance off course.
outline: Basic T to glass: what moved where
PFD areas and FMA
EADI and EHSI and their modern equivalents
EICAS and ECAM layout, colour code, failure flags
Trend arrow and CDI calculations
answer: From dials to screens. The basic six (airspeed, attitude, altimeter, turn coordinator, heading, vertical speed) were separate dials in the basic T. An EFIS draws them on screens from display computers fed by the air data and inertial units.

head: Area
Content
rows: attitude: sky, ground, horizon, pitch ladder, aircraft symbol, flight director bars, ILS deviation
airspeed tape, speed box, selected-speed bug, limit bands, 10 s speed trend arrow
altitude tape, selected altitude, barometric setting, vertical speed scale
flight mode annunciator: active and armed autopilot, autothrust and flight director modes

answer: EADI and EHSI. In the first EFIS (Boeing 757 and 767, Airbus A310) the EADI showed attitude, flight director, ILS deviation, radio altitude and a fast-or-slow pointer; the EHSI showed a compass rose with course, CDI, distance and wind, in map, VOR, approach and plan modes. Today the PFD's attitude area does the EADI's job and the navigation display does the EHSI's job, adding route, weather radar, traffic and terrain.

EICAS (Boeing). Upper screen: primary engine values (N1 or EPR, EGT) and crew alert messages; lower screen: secondary engine values (N2, fuel flow, oil, vibration) or synoptics. ECAM (Airbus). Engine and warning display above a system display; a failure brings up its procedure and the matching synoptic.

Colour and validity. Red: warning, immediate action, with master warning and sound. Amber: caution (Boeing also shows advisories in amber, indented). Green: normal or engaged. White: labels and memos. Invalid data is replaced by a failure flag, and a failed screen's page reverts to another screen; standby instruments remain the last layer.

answer.pre:
Δv = a × t = 0.9 kt/s × 10 s = 9 kt
tip  = 160 + 9 = 169 kt, pointing up the tape

deviation = 2 dots × 5° per dot = 10°
d = 30 NM × sin 10° = 30 × 0.1736 = 5.21 NM

answer: The needle is right, so the selected radial lies to the right and the pilot turns right to rejoin it.

Why the split. The PFD holds what is needed every second to fly, in the centre of the scan; the navigation display holds where the aircraft is going; the engine and alert screens hold system health and show detail only when something is abnormal. This keeps the primary scan short.
Closing check. Small-angle estimate: 30 × 10 × π ÷ 180 = 5.24 NM, close to 5.21 NM; 160 + 9 = 169 kt.

bank.q: Explain the ARINC 429 word format, signalling and topology, and how a receiver knows a word is valid. A transmitter sends 15 labels at 25 words/s each and 30 labels at 5 words/s each. Find the bus load at high and low speed, and the parity bit for a word whose first 31 bits contain seventeen 1s.
outline: One transmitter, up to 20 receivers, twisted pair
Bipolar return-to-zero, ±10 V
32-bit fields: label, SDI, data, SSM, parity
Validity: parity, SSM, label, timing
Load calculation and parity
answer: Topology. One transmitter drives a shielded twisted pair and up to 20 receivers listen. A reply needs a second pair with its own transmitter. One pair carries many parameters, each tagged by a label.

Signalling. Bipolar return-to-zero: a 1 is +10 V (HI) for the first half bit then NULL, a 0 is −10 V (LO) then NULL. The return to NULL in every bit lets the receiver recover the clock. Speeds: 100 kbit/s high speed, 12 to 14.5 kbit/s low speed (12.5 kbit/s used here). At least 4 bit times of NULL separate words.

head: Bits
Field
Meaning
rows: parameter code in octal, sent first
which of two similar sources sent it
19 bits: BNR (bit 29 sign), BCD or discrete
BNR: 11 normal, 01 no computed data, 10 functional test, 00 failure warning

answer: Validity. The receiver accepts a word only if the parity is odd, the label is one it expects, the SSM says normal operation, and the word arrives within its expected refresh time; otherwise the value is flagged invalid and the display shows a failure flag.

answer.pre:
T<sub>w</sub> = 36 bits ÷ 100 000 bit/s = 0.36 ms
load = 525 × 0.36 ms = 189 ms per second = 18.9 %

T<sub>w</sub> = 36 ÷ 12 500 = 2.88 ms
load = 525 × 2.88 ms = 1512 ms per second = 151 %  → does not fit

answer: Parity. Seventeen 1s is already odd, so bit 32 is 0.

Why two speeds. Low speed suits slowly changing data over long cables with less radiated interference and cheaper receivers; high speed suits flight-critical and fast-changing data such as attitude and air data, which displays and the autopilot need many times a second.

BNR data. In binary (BNR) words the value is a two's complement fraction of a stated range, with bit 29 as the sign and bit 28 as the most significant bit. The resolution is the range divided by 2 to the power of the number of data bits used, so a parameter that needs finer resolution uses more of bits 11 to 28.

Electrical rejection of noise. The receiver reads the difference between the two wires of the twisted pair. Interference from nearby cables couples almost equally into both wires and cancels in the difference, which is why the pair is twisted and shielded.
Closing check. 1 ÷ 0.36 ms = 2778 words/s maximum at high speed and 525 ÷ 2778 = 18.9 %; at low speed the maximum is 347 words/s, below 525.

bank.q: Describe the word types, terminals and message formats of MIL-STD-1553B. A bus controller polls 6 remote terminals every 20 ms, each sending 8 data words to the BC; the response time is 6 µs and the intermessage gap 4 µs. Find the message time and bus load, and the time of an RT-to-RT transfer of 4 data words.
outline: 1 Mbit/s, Manchester II, dual redundant
Command, data and status words; 20 bit times
BC, RT, bus monitor
Receive, transmit and RT-to-RT sequences
Timing table and load
answer: Physical layer. 1 Mbit/s on a shielded twisted pair with transformer-coupled stubs; Manchester II coding puts a transition in the middle of each bit so the clock travels with the data. Normally two cables, A and B; the BC retries on the other bus after a failure.

Words. Each word is 20 bit times = 20 µs: 3-bit sync, 16 bits, odd parity. Command word: RT address (5 bits), transmit/receive bit, subaddress (5 bits), word count (5 bits, 1 to 32 words). Status word: RT address and flags (message error, busy, subsystem flag, terminal flag). Data word: 16 data bits.
Terminals. One bus controller starts every transfer; up to 31 remote terminals reply only when commanded, within 4 to 12 µs; a bus monitor records traffic without replying.

Formats. BC to RT (receive): command, data words, then RT status. RT to BC (transmit): command, RT status, then data words. RT to RT: receive command to the destination, transmit command to the source, source status and data, then destination status. Broadcast and mode-code messages also exist.

answer.pre:
6 messages × 210 µs = 1260 µs every 20 000 µs
load = 1260 ÷ 20 000 = 6.3 %

answer: Interpretation. At 6.3 % load the BC has plenty of time left for aperiodic messages and retries. Overhead per message is 50 µs (command, response, status, gap), so short messages are inefficient: one data word costs 70 µs.

Why command/response suits military aircraft. Every transfer is confirmed by a status word, so the BC knows at once if a terminal failed to answer and can retry on the other cable or mark the terminal failed. The BC's fixed schedule makes the timing predictable, and adding a terminal needs only a stub on the existing cable.
Efficiency with longer messages. A 32-word transmit message takes 20 + 6 + 20 + 640 + 4 = 690 µs for 512 data bits, about 0.74 Mbit/s of useful data, against 1 Mbit/s on the wire.

bank.q: An aircraft's new display system moves from ARINC 429 to AFDX. Its end system needs three virtual links: VLa with Lmax 500 bytes and BAG 4 ms, VLb with 1518 bytes and 2 ms, and VLc with 128 bytes and 1 ms. Find each reserved bandwidth, the port load on a 100 Mbit/s link, the wire time of a VLb frame with 20 bytes of overhead, and the largest BAG for a parameter needed 50 times a second. Explain what guarantee the network gives and how redundancy works.
outline: Why ARINC 429 runs out
End system, switch, virtual link
B = 8 × Lmax ÷ BAG for each VL; total and load
Wire time; BAG from update rate
Policing, bounded delay, networks A and B, sequence numbers
answer: Why change. ARINC 429 gives 100 kbit/s one way per pair; a modern display system needs megabits per second both ways between many computers, which would need hundreds of pairs.

Parts. Each computer has an end system; switches forward frames only to their destinations; links are full duplex, so there are no collisions. A virtual link is a one-way path from one source to one or more destinations, with Lmax (64 to 1518 bytes) and BAG (1 to 128 ms, powers of two) fixed in a configuration table.
Port load. 8.096 ÷ 100 = 8.1 % of the link.
BAG from update rate. 50 times a second needs a frame at least every 1 ÷ 50 = 20 ms. BAG must be a power of two not larger than 20 ms, so BAG = 16 ms (32 ms would give only 31.25 frames/s).

Guarantee. The switch polices each VL against its BAG and Lmax and drops frames that break the contract, and the end system limits output jitter to 500 µs. Because every VL's worst case is known, the worst-case delay through every switch can be computed before flight. The network guarantees a bound on delay and on bandwidth, not an average.

Redundancy. Each end system sends every frame on two independent networks, A and B, with a per-VL sequence number. The receiver keeps the first valid copy and drops the duplicate, so one failed switch or cut cable loses nothing.

Sizing rule. Choose each VL's Lmax from the largest message it carries (plus headers), and its BAG from the fastest update rate needed, rounding down to a power of two. Then add every VL that leaves each port and check the sum stays well below the link rate, here 8.1 %, leaving room for growth and for the worst-case queues at the switch outputs.
Migration path. Old ARINC 429 sources need not be replaced at once: a remote data concentrator or gateway reads their labels and packs them into AFDX frames on a suitable virtual link.

bank.q: Design the measurement chain for a hydraulic pressure transducer of range 0 to 25 MPa. It is a full bridge of four 350 Ω gauges, gauge factor 2.0, excited by 5 V, with ±800 µε at full scale. It feeds an instrumentation amplifier (R = 25 kΩ) and a 12-bit ADC with Vref = 2.5 V sampled at 200 Hz. Choose the gain resistor for about 2.4 V full scale, find the codes at full scale and at 20.7 MPa, the pressure per code, and an anti-alias filter.
outline: Bridge output from GF, strain and excitation
Instrumentation amplifier gain and R<sub>G</sub> (standard value)
ADC resolution, full-scale code and code at 20.7 MPa
Pressure per code
Anti-alias RC filter below 100 Hz
Why each block is needed

answer.pre:
ΔR = GF × ε × R = 2.0 × 800 × 10⁻⁶ × 350 = 0.56 Ω
full bridge: V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>ex</sub> × ΔR ÷ R = 5 × 0.56 ÷ 350 = 8.0 mV at 25 MPa
sensitivity = 8.0 mV ÷ 25 MPa = 0.32 mV/MPa

answer: Why a full bridge. Four active arms give four times the output of one gauge, a linear output, and cancel temperature changes that affect all arms equally.

answer.pre:
wanted G = 2.4 V ÷ 8.0 mV = 300
G = 1 + 2R ÷ R<sub>G</sub>  →  R<sub>G</sub> = 2 × 25 000 ÷ 299 = 167.2 Ω
standard 169 Ω → G = 1 + 50 000 ÷ 169 = 296.9
full-scale output = 8.0 mV × 296.9 = 2.375 V  (below 2.5 V: no clipping)

answer: Why an instrumentation amplifier. The bridge output is a few millivolts riding on 2.5 V of common-mode voltage. The instrumentation amplifier's inputs do not load the bridge and it amplifies only the difference.

answer.pre:
Q = 2.5 ÷ 2¹² = 2.5 ÷ 4096 = 0.6104 mV
full-scale code = floor(2.375 ÷ 0.0006104) = 3890
pressure per code = 25 MPa ÷ 3890 = 6.43 kPa

answer: Anti-alias filter. At 200 Hz sampling, anything above 100 Hz aliases. A first-order RC with R = 10 kΩ and C = 220 nF gives fc = 1 ÷ (2π × 10 000 × 220 × 10⁻⁹) = 72.3 Hz, below 100 Hz; hydraulic pressure changes far more slowly, so the signal passes. A higher-order filter or faster sampling would reject pump ripple better.

Software. The microcontroller converts code to pressure, applies a calibration (offset and gain, and temperature correction), checks range and rate limits, and sends the value with a validity status on the bus.

Ratiometric measurement. If the bridge excitation and the ADC reference come from the same source, a drift in that source changes the bridge output and the step size Q by the same fraction, so the code does not change. Otherwise a 1 % drift in the 5 V excitation gives a 1 % pressure error (0.25 MPa at full scale).

Resolution and error budget. Quantisation alone gives at most one code of error with the rounding-down rule, 6.43 kPa, which is 0.026 % of 25 MPa. In practice the larger errors are the gauge temperature drift, the amplifier offset (a 100 µV input offset times 296.9 gives 29.7 mV at the output, about 49 codes or 0.31 MPa) and the gain-resistor tolerance, so the unit is calibrated at zero and full scale and the offset is subtracted in software.

Protection. Series resistors and clamp diodes at the amplifier inputs protect against spikes on the long sensor cable, and the cable is shielded and twisted so that interference appears as common-mode voltage, which the instrumentation amplifier rejects.
Closing check. 3221 × 25 ÷ 3890 = 20.70 MPa, the input pressure.

bank.q: With circuits, explain the inverting, non-inverting and differential op-amp amplifiers and the transistor relay driver with a flyback diode. Use Rf = 47 kΩ and Rin = 4.7 kΩ with a 0.25 V input; a differential amplifier with 10 kΩ and 100 kΩ resistors fed with 2.512 V and 2.500 V; and a 28 V, 140 Ω relay coil switched by an NPN transistor (β ≥ 50) from a 3.3 V microcontroller pin.
outline: Ideal op-amp rules
Inverting and non-inverting gains with outputs
Differential amplifier: gain and common-mode rejection
BJT in saturation: I<sub>C</sub>, I<sub>B</sub>, R<sub>B</sub>
Flyback diode orientation and purpose
answer: Ideal rules. With negative feedback, no current enters the inputs and the output drives the two inputs to the same voltage.

answer.text: Inverting amplifier (signal through Rin to the − input, Rf from output to −, + grounded).
Non-inverting amplifier (signal to +, Rf from output to −, Rin from − to ground).

answer: A voltage follower is the non-inverting circuit with the output tied straight to the − input: gain 1, very high input resistance, used as a buffer.

answer.text: Differential amplifier (R1 = R3 = 10 kΩ, R2 = R4 = 100 kΩ).
answer.pre:
gain = R2 ÷ R1 = 10
V<sub>out</sub> = 10 × (2.512 − 2.500) = 10 × 0.012 = 0.12 V
common-mode part 2.506 V is rejected (as well as the resistor match allows)

answer: This is the job a bridge needs: a small difference on top of a large common voltage. The three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier adds high input resistance and one-resistor gain setting.

answer.pre:
I<sub>C</sub> = 28 V ÷ 140 Ω = 0.20 A
minimum I<sub>B</sub> = 0.20 ÷ 50 = 4 mA; ×2 for saturation → 8 mA
R<sub>B</sub> = (3.3 − 0.7) ÷ 0.008 = 325 Ω → standard 330 Ω gives 2.6 ÷ 330 = 7.9 mA

answer: In saturation V<sub>CE</sub> is about 0.2 V, so the transistor dissipates about 0.2 × 0.20 = 0.04 W. The pin must be able to source about 8 mA; if not, a MOSFET (driven by gate voltage, almost no gate current) is used instead.

Flyback diode. Fitted across the coil, cathode to +28 V, anode to the collector. When the transistor turns off, the coil current (0.20 A) flows round through the diode instead of producing a spike of L di/dt that would break down the transistor. Fitted backwards it would short the supply each time the coil is on.

bank.q: Explain how temperature is measured on an engine and in its oil system with thermocouples, RTDs and thermistors. Four type K EGT probes read 700, 720, 690 and 730 °C. An EGT thermocouple gives 28.0 mV with the cold junction at 35 °C (take 41 µV/°C). A Pt100 (α = 0.00385 /°C) in the oil reads 138.5 Ω. Find the average EGT, the compensated EGT and the oil temperature.
outline: Seebeck effect, hot and cold junctions
Cold-junction compensation
Parallel probes give an average
RTD law and thermistor contrast
Calculations and the error without compensation
answer: Thermocouple. Two dissimilar metals (chromel and alumel for type K) joined at the hot end give an emf that depends on the difference between the hot junction and the cold junction, where the wires meet the instrument's copper. It is active (needs no supply), rugged and works to over 1000 °C, so it suits exhaust gas temperature.

Cold-junction compensation. The instrument measures its own terminal temperature and adds the emf the thermocouple would give at that temperature. Without it the reading is low by the cold-junction temperature and drifts as the instrument warms.
Averaging. Several probes round the exhaust are wired in parallel; with equal loop resistances the indicator sees the average emf, so a hot or cold streak at one probe does not dominate.

answer.pre:
ΔT = 28.0 × 10⁻³ ÷ 41 × 10⁻⁶ = 682.9 °C
T<sub>hot</sub> = 682.9 + 35 = 717.9 °C
without compensation the gauge would show 682.9 °C, 35 °C low

answer: The 41 µV/°C sensitivity is a classroom approximation; real indicators use the type K reference table because the emf is not exactly linear.

RTD. A platinum element whose resistance rises almost linearly: RT = R₀(1 + αT). It is passive (needs a small excitation current), accurate and stable from about −200 to 600 °C, and suits oil, fuel and air temperatures.

Thermistor. A semiconductor bead whose resistance falls steeply and non-linearly with temperature (NTC). It is very sensitive but has a narrow range, so it is used for cabin and equipment-bay temperatures, not EGT.

Choosing the sensor. EGT needs a thermocouple (range, ruggedness, no supply); oil and fuel temperatures need the accuracy and stability of an RTD; a thermistor fits where a cheap, sensitive sensor over a narrow range is enough. The RTD is read by passing a small known current and measuring the voltage, kept small to avoid self-heating.

bank.q: Explain how a head-up display produces a collimated image, the difference between conformal and non-conformal symbols, and why boresight alignment matters. On an approach at 150 kt ground speed and 800 ft/min descent, the HUD aperture is 130 mm at 550 mm from the eye. Find the flight path angle and the instantaneous field of view, and the symbol error of an HMD with 20 ms latency at 150°/s head rate.
outline: Parts: computer, source, collimating optics, combiner
Image at infinity; no refocus between symbols and scene
Conformal and non-conformal symbols, FPV
γ, IFOV and HMD latency calculations
Boresight and civil and military uses
answer: Parts. The HUD computer builds the symbols from air data, inertial and guidance data; the display source draws them; the collimating optics have the source at their focal plane so each point leaves as parallel rays; the combiner reflects the display colour to the eye and passes the outside scene.

Collimation. Parallel rays form a virtual image at infinity, the same focus as the runway, so the pilot reads symbols without refocusing or looking down. A panel at 0.75 m would need 1.33 dioptres of refocus each time.
Symbols. Conformal: horizon, pitch ladder, runway outline and flight path vector, drawn on the real objects. Non-conformal: airspeed, altitude, heading and mode labels at fixed places.

answer.pre:
V<sub>g</sub> = 150 × 101.27 = 15 190 ft/min
γ = arctan(800 ÷ 15 190) = arctan(0.0527) = 3.01° below the horizon

IFOV = 2 arctan(130 ÷ (2 × 550)) = 2 arctan(0.1182) = 2 × 6.74° = 13.48°
half-angle 6.74° > 3.01°, so the FPV is in view

answer: Boresight. The HUD must be aligned with the aircraft axes; if it is off by even a fraction of a degree, the FPV points at the wrong place on the runway and a hand-flown low-visibility landing is guided to the wrong spot. HUDs are aligned on installation and checked against the aircraft datum.

answer.pre:
error = 150 °/s × 0.020 s = 3.0°
for 0.5°: latency ≤ 0.5 ÷ 150 = 3.3 ms, or head-motion prediction

answer: Uses. Civil: low-visibility approach and landing, often with an enhanced vision image. Military: weapon aiming, off-boresight cueing through the HMD, night flying; the F-35 uses its HMD in place of a HUD.

HMD versus HUD. The HMD keeps symbols in view wherever the head turns, which a fixed HUD cannot, but it adds helmet mass, needs a head tracker of low latency and must stay safe in an ejection. Conformal HMD symbols are only as good as the tracker.
Limits of a HUD. Too many symbols clutter the view, and brightness must follow the outside light so the symbols neither vanish against a bright sky nor hide the runway at night.

bank.q: Compare ARINC 429, MIL-STD-1553B and AFDX as data networks for a transport aircraft, with numbers for their data throughput, and justify a choice for flight-critical data and for passenger-cabin data.
outline: Topology, direction, speed, coding of each
Throughput: 429 word, 1553B 32-word message, AFDX 1518-byte frame
Determinism and redundancy of each
Weight and wiring
Choice for flight-critical and cabin data with reasons

head: Feature
ARINC 429
MIL-STD-1553B
AFDX
rows: BAG and Lmax policed per VL
networks A and B, sequence numbers

answer.pre:
19 data bits per 36 bit times at 100 kbit/s
19 ÷ 0.36 ms = 52.8 kbit/s of data per pair

answer.text: 1553B, one 32-word transmit message (8 µs response, 4 µs gap).
AFDX, 1518-byte frames back to back (20 bytes overhead each).
answer.pre:
wire time = 1538 × 8 ÷ 10⁸ = 123.0 µs
frame rate ≈ 1518 × 8 ÷ 123.0 µs = 98.7 Mbit/s of frame bits

answer: Throughput comparison. AFDX carries roughly 130 times the useful rate of a 1553B bus and about 1900 times one ARINC 429 pair, and it does so in both directions on every link.

Wiring. ARINC 429 needs a pair for every transmitter, so a large aircraft has hundreds of pairs; 1553B shares one dual cable among many terminals; AFDX uses one link pair per end-system port per network, through switches, which cuts weight sharply on a big aircraft.

Flight-critical data. AFDX is the choice for the backbone: bandwidth reserved per virtual link, worst-case delay computable before flight, switches that police faulty senders, and two independent networks. Simple sensors and older LRUs stay on ARINC 429, joined through gateways or remote data concentrators. 1553B is a military bus; on a civil transport its certification base and supply chain are weaker, though it remains a fair choice on military transports.

Cabin data. In-flight entertainment and passenger connectivity need high, bursty bandwidth but no flight-safety guarantee. They go on ordinary Ethernet, kept separate from the AFDX domain by a one-way or filtered gateway, so cabin traffic or a cyber attack from a passenger device cannot reach flight-critical networks.
Judgement. The right answer is a layered network, not a single bus: AFDX core, ARINC 429 at the edges, and a separated open network for the cabin.

Certification and cost. ARINC 429 parts are cheap, simple and proven, so an LRU that only broadcasts a few values stays on 429. AFDX switches and end systems cost more and need a network-wide configuration and timing analysis, which pays off only when many computers exchange a lot of data.

Error detection. ARINC 429 and 1553B check each word with one odd parity bit, which catches any single-bit error but not every multi-bit error; ARINC 429 adds the SSM status and 1553B adds the status word and retries. AFDX frames carry the 32-bit Ethernet CRC, and the sequence numbers reject duplicates and out-of-order frames, so its integrity checking is far stronger.

Latency. One ARINC 429 word takes 0.36 ms at high speed; a 1553B message of 4 data words takes about 132 µs plus its wait in the BC's schedule; an AFDX frame waits at most one BAG at the source plus the computed switch delays. For a fly-by-wire loop running at 50 to 100 Hz, all three can be fast enough; the difference is how many signals each can carry at that rate.
Closing check. 98.7 ÷ 0.74 = 133 and 98 700 ÷ 52.8 = 1869, consistent with the ratios used.

bank.q: A display function whose loss is hazardous is hosted on an IMA module beside a cabin function with no safety effect. Evaluate the software levels, the partitioning needed, and the verification effort. Map its development onto the V-model, give an MC/DC test set for the decision (a or b) and c if it were level A, and assess a traceability review that finds 114 of 120 low-level requirements traced to tests.
outline: Levels from failure conditions: hazardous B, no effect E
Robust partitioning; module and OS at the higher level
V-model mapping and two-way traceability
Coverage by level; MC/DC set of n + 1 tests
Traceability percentage and gaps; verdict
answer: Levels. Software level follows the failure condition: hazardous gives level B, no safety effect gives level E. The display partition must meet the level B objectives (65 in DO-178B, with decision coverage); the cabin partition has no objectives.

Partitioning. The two may share the module only if ARINC 653 robust partitioning holds: the cabin partition gets a fixed time window and protected memory, so it cannot overrun its slot, write into the display partition's memory or crash the module. The operating system, the module hardware and the partition configuration must be assured to the higher level, B, because their failure could take the display down.

head: Left arm (define)
Right arm (verify)
rows: System requirements for the display function
Hardware/software integration tests on the IMA module
High-level software requirements (what to show, timing)

answer: Traceability runs both ways: down, so every requirement has code and tests; up, so no code exists without a requirement. Robustness tests with abnormal inputs are added.

answer.text: MC/DC set for (a or b) and c, if level A.

answer: Each pair differs in one condition only and flips the outcome, so 4 tests (n + 1 for n = 3) replace the 8 of exhaustive testing. At level B decision coverage would need only two tests with opposite outcomes, such as T1 and T2.

answer.pre:
traced = 114 ÷ 120 × 100 = 95 %
gaps = 120 − 114 = 6 requirements without a traced test

answer: Verdict. The evidence is incomplete. Each of the 6 requirements needs a test traced to it, or the requirement must be shown unnecessary and removed through the change process, before the level B objectives are met. 95 % is not a pass mark; the target is 100 %.

Evaluation. Hosting a level E function beside a level B one saves a box, but it adds the cost of assuring the platform and the partitioning to level B. The saving is worth it when many functions share the module; for a single small cabin function, a separate module may be simpler.

Independence and process. At levels A and B some verification must be done by people independent of the authors, and the plans, configuration management records and quality assurance records must show exactly which version of the code and data was verified and loaded. On IMA the configuration tables (partition windows, memory maps, virtual links) are themselves verified data items.

Structural coverage by level. Level A: MC/DC; level B: decision coverage; level C: statement coverage; level D: none. Coverage analysis also finds dead code (no requirement) and missing tests (requirement without test), which links back to the traceability review.
Closing check. (a or b) and c: T1 = (1 or 0) and 1 = 1; T2 = (0 or 0) and 1 = 0; T3 = (0 or 1) and 1 = 1; T4 = (1 or 0) and 0 = 0. 114 + 6 = 120.

glossary.def: All the electronic systems of an aircraft or spacecraft that sense, compute, communicate, navigate, control or display.
Size, weight and power: the budget that limits UAV and military avionics.
Fault detection, isolation and recovery: on-board logic that finds a fault and switches to a spare.
What a platform carries to do its job: sensors, communication relays, weapons, science instruments or passengers.
One dedicated box per function with point-to-point wiring.
Shared cabinets of plug-in modules hosting many functions as protected software partitions.
A box that can be removed and replaced on the flight line.
The repeating cycle in which every ARINC 653 partition gets its time window.
Built-in test equipment: self-test inside a box that stores and reports fault codes.
The standard layout of the six flight instruments with the attitude indicator at the top centre.
Electronic flight instrument system: display units, display computers and control panels.
Moving a failed screen's page to another screen.
A PFD arrow pointing to the airspeed expected in 10 seconds.
Engine indication and crew alerting system (Boeing).
Electronic centralised aircraft monitor (Airbus).
The partly reflecting glass of a HUD that overlays symbols on the outside view.
A HUD symbol drawn where the real object is, such as the horizon or flight path vector.
The sensor that measures where an HMD wearer's head points.
The 8-bit octal code at the start of an ARINC 429 word that names the parameter.
Sign/status matrix: bits 30 and 31 of an ARINC 429 word.
The one 1553B terminal that starts every transfer.
A 1553B terminal that replies only when commanded.
A code with a transition in the middle of every bit, so the clock travels with the data.
A one-way AFDX path with a reserved bandwidth set by BAG and Lmax.
Bandwidth allocation gap: the minimum time between frame starts on one virtual link.
Reflection of light at a boundary to a lower-index medium beyond the critical angle; it guides light in a fibre.
Modified condition/decision coverage: each condition shown to change the decision on its own.
Links from each requirement to its design, code and tests, in both directions.
Four resistive arms with excitation across one diagonal and output across the other.
Adding the emf for the reference-junction temperature to a thermocouple reading.
Linear variable differential transformer: an AC position sensor with a movable core.
A three-op-amp differential amplifier with high input resistance and gain set by one resistor.
High frequencies appearing as false low frequencies when sampling is too slow.
A timer that resets a microcontroller if its software stops responding.
